```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 05 - Time Series and Causal Inference](../../Notebooks/Part%2005%20-%20Time%20Series%20and%20Causal%20Inference/Part%2005%20-%20Time%20Series%20and%20Causal%20Inference.ipynb).
It turns posting histories into time series, describes their rhythms,
and then asks a harder question: did a real-world event *cause* a change
in behavior? The same two quasi-experimental designs — interrupted time
series and difference-in-differences — are fit here with base R's `lm()`
in place of statsmodels.

Both versions analyze **the same saved archive**, so they should agree
exactly. Section 5 checks that they do: R's regression coefficients are
compared with the table the Python notebook saved.

Every post, reply, and repost on Bluesky carries a timestamp, which
means an account's feed is more than a pile of content: it is a
**behavioral trace over time**. Fifteen years of Twitter research showed
how much social science lives inside those traces. Golder & Macy (2011)
found that mood follows daily and seasonal rhythms across cultures by
timestamping millions of tweets, Dodds et al. (2011) built a real-time
"hedonometer" of collective happiness, and González-Bailón et al. (2011)
reconstructed the minute-by-minute dynamics of protest recruitment
during Spain's 15-M movement.

Time series also let us ask a more ambitious kind of question. When
something happens in the world (an election, a platform migration, a
policy change), we want to know whether behavior changed *because of
it*. A line that goes up after an event is not an answer: posting might
have been trending upward already, the change might be seasonal, or
something else might have happened at the same time. Answering causal
questions with observational data requires **research designs**, not
just plots. This document introduces two workhorse designs from the
quasi-experimental toolkit:

* **Interrupted time series (ITS)**: model the pre-event trend, and ask
  whether the level or slope of the series breaks at the event.
* **Difference-in-differences (DiD)**: compare the before–after change
  for a "treated" unit against the before–after change for a comparison
  unit that was *not* affected by the event.

Both designs come from the program-evaluation toolkit that economists
and epidemiologists reach for when randomized experiments are
impossible. If causal inference is new to you, two free online
textbooks pair well with this document: Scott Cunningham's [*Causal
Inference: The Mixtape*](https://mixtape.scunning.com/) and Nick
Huntington-Klein's [*The Effect*](https://theeffectbook.net/). We apply
both designs to a genuine **natural experiment** (an event whose timing
was determined by outside forces rather than by the people whose
behavior we measure): the surge of new users and activity that hit
Bluesky after the U.S. presidential election on November 5, 2024. And we
will be candid about where the designs succeed and where they fail.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this document you will be able to:

1. Page backward through an account's **posting history**, decide when
   to stop, and analyze a saved archive.
2. Parse ISO-8601 timestamps into **timezone-aware** date-times and
   reason about UTC versus local time.
3. Turn an event log into daily and weekly counts, smooth with rolling
   means, and describe diurnal and weekly rhythms.
4. Specify and interpret an **interrupted time series (segmented)
   regression** with `lm()`, including its autocorrelation caveats.
5. Build a tidy two-account panel and estimate a
   **difference-in-differences** regression, and diagnose when the
   parallel-trends assumption fails.
6. Retrieve **profile covariates** to reason about matching a better
   comparison group.
7. Articulate the **threats to validity** (selection, anticipation,
   concurrent shocks) that separate causal claims from correlational ones.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

Both causal designs ultimately boil down to one call to `lm()`, R's
ordinary least squares regression (the same line-fitting workhorse from
introductory statistics), applied to carefully constructed columns.
[broom](https://broom.tidymodels.org/)'s `tidy()` turns a fitted model
into a tibble of coefficients, and
[lubridate](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/) handles dates and time
zones.

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. Most
parts gate *every* chunk on that flag, because bskyr needs credentials
for every call. This part is different. The analysis runs on a saved
archive, so it works **without** credentials; only the chunks that call
the API (re-collecting the archive, matching, keyword search) are gated
on `bsky_authed`.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
```

## 1. Collecting posting histories, and why we analyze a saved archive

The event we will study is the November 2024 US election and the surge
of Twitter-to-Bluesky migration that followed it. We need two histories
that reach well back before the event: a *treated* account (The New York
Times, a newsroom whose Bluesky audience exploded during the surge) and a
*comparison* account (`bsky.app`, the platform's official account).

**An author feed is returned newest first.** To reach November 2024 we
have to page through *everything* the account has posted since, and a
newsroom keeps posting every day. In mid-2026 a fixed budget of about
40,000 items reached comfortably past the event. By November 2026 the
same budget stopped two months *after* it, the pre-event period silently
disappeared, and every causal estimate failed. A collection designed
around today's data ages, sometimes in months.

So this document separates **collecting** from **analyzing**:

* By default it reads the **archive saved by the Python notebook**,
  `actions.csv.gz`: one row per action, keeping only the account, the
  action type, a reply flag, and the timestamp (data minimization: no
  URIs, no text, no engagement counts). Every number below is then
  reproducible.
* With the environment variable `PART05_REFRESH=1` set and credentials
  available, the `refresh` chunk re-collects the archive with bskyr and
  writes it next to this document instead. That takes about 500
  requests, which is why it is opt-in.

```{r params, eval=TRUE}
TREATED <- "nytimes.com"
COMPARISON <- "bsky.app"
EVENT <- as_date("2024-11-05")
TZ <- "America/New_York"

SHARED_ARCHIVE <- file.path("..", "..", "Notebooks",
                            "Part 05 - Time Series and Causal Inference",
                            "data", "actions.csv.gz")
LOCAL_ARCHIVE <- file.path("data", "actions.csv.gz")

REFRESH <- Sys.getenv("PART05_REFRESH") == "1"
```

The refresh pages through each account's history with
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html), sizing its budget
from the post count in [`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html). It reads
raw API pages (`clean = FALSE`), so it can classify
each feed item directly: an item with a `reason` of type
`#reasonRepost` is a repost, and it is timestamped by *when the account
reposted* (`reason$indexedAt`) rather than when the original post was
written. A reply is a post whose record carries a `reply` field.

```{r refresh, eval = bsky_authed && REFRESH}
budget_items <- function(actor) {
  # One item per post, ~25% extra for reposts, plus slack
  ceiling(bs_get_profile(actor)$posts_count * 1.25) + 2000
}

collect_actions <- function(actor) {
  pages <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, limit = budget_items(actor), clean = FALSE)
  items <- list_flatten(map(pages, "feed"))
  map(items, \(item) {
    is_repost <- identical(item$reason$`$type`, "app.bsky.feed.defs#reasonRepost")
    tibble(
      actor = actor,
      action = if (is_repost) "repost" else "post",
      is_reply = !is.null(item$post$record$reply),
      created_at = if (is_repost) item$reason$indexedAt else item$post$record$createdAt
    )
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
bind_rows(collect_actions(TREATED), collect_actions(COMPARISON)) |>
  mutate(created_at = format(ymd_hms(created_at, tz = "UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")) |>
  arrange(actor, created_at) |>
  write_csv(LOCAL_ARCHIVE)
```

```{r load, eval=TRUE}
ARCHIVE <- if (REFRESH && file.exists(LOCAL_ARCHIVE)) LOCAL_ARCHIVE else SHARED_ARCHIVE

archive_metadata <- read_json(file.path(dirname(SHARED_ARCHIVE), "collection_metadata.json"))
archive_metadata$collected_at

read_csv(ARCHIVE, show_col_types = FALSE) |> head()
```

Each row is one action, stored with its timestamp as a UTC string (the
trailing `Z`). The archive reaches back to November 2023 for
`nytimes.com`, a full year before the event, and stops there by design.
An author feed is more than original posts: each item can be an original
post, a reply, or a repost, and the archive records an `action` type for
each. Reposts are timestamped by *when the account reposted*, because
the act of reposting is the behavior we want to place in time.

## 2. Timestamps and timezones

API timestamps are UTC; humans live in local time, and diurnal rhythms
only make sense in the timezone where the humans behind the account
work — for a New York newsroom, Eastern time. We parse each timestamp
with `ymd_hms(tz = "UTC")` and convert it with `with_tz()`. We name the
*zone*, not an offset: the zone database knows New York is UTC−4 in
summer and UTC−5 in winter, so daylight-saving transitions are handled
for us.

```{r timestamps, eval=TRUE}
archive <- read_csv(ARCHIVE, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(created_at = with_tz(ymd_hms(created_at, tz = "UTC"), TZ)) |>
  arrange(created_at)

treated_posts <- filter(archive, actor == TREATED)
comparison_posts <- filter(archive, actor == COMPARISON)

first_action <- treated_posts$created_at[1]
c(local = format(first_action, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"),
  utc = format(with_tz(first_action, "UTC"), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"))

count(treated_posts, action)
sum(treated_posts$is_reply)
```

The first line shows one instant in two zones: converting between them
loses nothing. Original posts dominate: reposts are under a tenth of the
newsroom's activity, and replies are rare. An institutional account
broadcasts; it seldom converses. Still, "posting activity" is a bundle
of distinct behaviors. We analyze **all actions together** as one
measure of activity; everything below could be re-run on
`filter(treated_posts, action == "post")` to isolate original posting,
and checking whether your findings survive that choice is exactly the
kind of robustness check reviewers ask for (Exercise 2).

## 3. Descriptive time series: the rhythms of posting

Before any causal modeling, *look at the data*. The raw records are an
**event log**: one row per action, at irregular instants. Most
time-series tools instead want a **time series** proper: one number per
regular interval (per day, per week). Grouping the event log into
fixed-width time bins and counting within each bin is called
**resampling**.

### Daily counts and a rolling mean

Counting actions per day gives a noisy series; a *rolling mean* smooths
it so the trend is visible. Two details: `complete()` fills in
zero-count days (a day with no posts is data, not a gap!), and
`stats::filter()` with equal weights of 1/k computes a centered k-day
moving average — base R's one-line rolling mean:

```{r daily, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
daily_counts <- function(posts) {
  posts |>
    count(date = as_date(created_at, tz = TZ)) |>
    complete(date = seq(min(date), max(date), by = "day"),
             fill = list(n = 0))
}

rolling_mean <- function(x, k = 28) {
  as.numeric(stats::filter(x, rep(1 / k, k), sides = 2))
}

treated_daily <- daily_counts(treated_posts)

treated_daily |>
  mutate(rolling = rolling_mean(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = n), color = "lightsteelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rolling), color = "navy", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Actions per day",
       title = paste("Daily activity:", TREATED),
       subtitle = "28-day centered rolling mean in navy") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Activity rises through spring 2024, sags to the lowest level of the
whole series in late summer and fall 2024, and then — in the weeks after
the November election — climbs to roughly four times its old level and
*stays there*. That is a **step**, not a spike: there is no decay back
toward the old baseline. The rolling mean makes that shape legible where
the raw daily series is just spiky noise. Keep it in mind: the entire
causal-inference half of this document is an attempt to put numbers,
and honest assumptions, around exactly this picture.

### Weekly counts

Weeks are the unit of analysis for the causal designs. To match the
Python notebook exactly, a week runs Monday through Sunday and is
labelled by its Sunday. That is what pandas' `resample('W')` does, and
here it is `floor_date(..., week_start = 1) + 6` days. We also drop the
final week, which is usually incomplete because collection happened
partway through it:

```{r weekly, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
weekly_counts <- function(posts) {
  posts |>
    mutate(week = as_date(floor_date(created_at, "week", week_start = 1), tz = TZ) + 6) |>
    count(week) |>
    complete(week = seq(min(week), max(week), by = "week"),
             fill = list(n = 0)) |>
    filter(week != max(week))          # drop the final, incomplete week
}

treated_weekly <- weekly_counts(treated_posts)

ggplot(treated_weekly, aes(week, n)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Weekly activity:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Even at a glance the series has two regimes, before and after late
2024; hold that thought for Section 4.

### Hour-of-day and day-of-week profiles

Golder & Macy (2011) showed that aggregate Twitter activity traces the
human day: people wake, work, and wind down on schedule, and their posts
follow. We can draw the same **diurnal profile** for one account, and
show why the timezone conversion mattered. The same actions binned by
local hour and by UTC hour tell two different stories, and only the
local one matches a plausible working day:

```{r rhythms, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
bind_rows(
  count(treated_posts, hour = hour(created_at)) |> mutate(clock = TZ),
  count(treated_posts, hour = hour(with_tz(created_at, "UTC"))) |> mutate(clock = "UTC")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour, n, color = clock)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 22, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day", y = "Total actions", color = NULL,
       title = paste("Diurnal profile:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()

treated_posts |>
  count(dow = wday(created_at, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(dow, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "navy", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Day of week", y = "Total actions",
       title = paste("Weekly rhythm:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

In New York time the account is quiet from midnight to about 6 AM and
peaks around midday — a newsroom's working day. The UTC curve is the
same data shifted by 4–5 hours. Weekend activity runs at about half the
weekday level, which is why the causal models use **weekly** counts:
summing over a full week removes the weekly cycle by construction.

### Year-over-year seasonality

```{r yoy, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
treated_posts |>
  count(year = factor(year(created_at)), month = month(created_at)) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, n, color = year)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Actions per month", color = "Year",
       title = paste("Year-over-year monthly activity:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Three years of data are too few to declare "seasonality" with
confidence: one account's annual pattern is confounded with everything
else that happened that year. What *is* unmistakable is that 2025 and
2026 sit far above 2024 in every month of the year. Something changed in
between.

## 4. An event: the November 2024 Bluesky surge

On **November 5, 2024**, Donald Trump won the U.S. presidential
election. In the days that followed, large numbers of users, disaffected
with X/Twitter and its owner's role in the campaign, migrated to
Bluesky. The platform [gained millions of users in roughly a
week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluesky#2024:_Growth), media outlets
covered the "X-odus", and activity from existing accounts spiked as
their timelines filled with new arrivals. For a researcher this is a
**natural experiment**: an event with a sharp, known onset that
plausibly changed behavior, but whose timing was not chosen by the
people whose behavior we measure.

Both designs compare against the pre-event period, so first we check that
we actually have one. Without it, the `post` indicator would be all ones,
the regression would be rank-deficient, and every estimate below would be
meaningless. This exact failure hit the live collection in November 2026:

```{r event-line, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
n_pre <- sum(treated_weekly$week < EVENT)
stopifnot("history does not reach far enough before the event" = n_pre >= 12)
c(pre_event_weeks = n_pre, post_event_weeks = nrow(treated_weekly) - n_pre)

ggplot(treated_weekly, aes(week, n)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Weekly activity with event line:", TREATED)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The break is real and it is where the story says it should be, though it
is not instantaneous. Weekly activity roughly doubles in the two weeks
after the election and keeps ramping for about seven weeks, into late
December, before leveling off around 400–450 actions a week. The
pre-event period isn't flat either: it rises through spring 2024 and
falls to a low just before the election, so the event arrives at a
seasonal trough. "The line goes up after the event" is journalism, not
causal inference. The question a causal design answers is: **how much of
the change is a break from where the pre-existing trend was already
heading?**

## 5. Interrupted time series

The interrupted time series (ITS) design, also called **segmented
regression**, formalizes that question. We model weekly counts as a
linear trend that is allowed to *break* at the event, in both level and
slope:

*y*<sub>t</sub> = β₀ + β₁·t + β₂·post<sub>t</sub> + β₃·(t − t<sub>event</sub>)·post<sub>t</sub> + ε<sub>t</sub>

where *t* counts weeks from the start of the series and post is 1 for
weeks on or after the event. Each coefficient has a direct
interpretation:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| β₀ | baseline level at the start of the series |
| β₁ | pre-event trend (actions per week, per week) |
| β₂ | **immediate level shift** at the event |
| β₃ | **change in slope** after the event |

Three vocabulary words recur in everything you will read about this
design:

* A **level shift** is an immediate jump (or drop) in the series at the
  event: the height of the line changes, captured by β₂.
* A **slope change** (or *trend change*) is a change in the steepness of
  the series after the event, captured by β₃. An event can produce
  either, both, or neither.
* The **counterfactual** is the path the series *would have taken* had
  the event never happened. We can never observe it (the *fundamental
  problem of causal inference*), so every design is, at heart, an
  argument for a particular stand-in. ITS's stand-in is the pre-event
  trend β₀ + β₁·t, extended forward. For a friendly, deeper treatment,
  see [Chapter 17 of *The Effect*](https://theeffectbook.net/ch-EventStudies.html).

Read the chunk below as building the regression's design matrix by hand,
column for column as in the Python notebook:

* `t` numbers the weeks 0, 1, 2, ...;
* `post` is 0 before the event and 1 from the first post-event week on;
* `t_post` is `t − t_event` in post-event weeks and 0 before, where
  `t_event` is the index of the first post-event week, so it counts
  weeks since the event, starting at 0.

`lm()` — R's workhorse linear-regression function — then fits the model:

```{r its, eval=TRUE}
its_data <- treated_weekly |>
  mutate(
    t = row_number() - 1,
    post = as.integer(week >= EVENT),
    t_post = (t - min(t[post == 1])) * post
  )

its_fit <- lm(n ~ t + post + t_post, data = its_data)

its_table <- broom::tidy(its_fit) |>
  mutate(term = c("intercept", "trend", "level_shift", "trend_change"))
its_table

pre_mean <- mean(its_data$n[its_data$post == 0])
coefs <- setNames(its_table$estimate, its_table$term)
```

Before the election the account averaged about
**`r round(pre_mean)` actions per week**, with a pre-event trend of
`r sprintf("%+.2f", coefs[["trend"]])` per week. That trend is
statistically indistinguishable from zero: the rise through spring and
the fall into autumn roughly cancel. At the event the level jumps by
**`r sprintf("%+.0f", coefs[["level_shift"]])` actions per week**, more
than three times the pre-event average. The slope afterward changes by
only `r sprintf("%+.2f", coefs[["trend_change"]])`, so the new level
*persists* instead of decaying. That is a sustained step: a change in
the account's regime, not a passing burst of attention. (These numbers
are computed inline from the fitted model, so they always match the
table above.)

One honest caveat about the model: a single straight line is a crude
summary of a pre-period that rose and then fell. Because the event
arrives at the bottom of the autumn dip, the jump is measured from a low
point. A model of the dip, or a window starting in summer 2024, would
report a smaller level shift.

### Does R agree with Python?

Both implementations read the same archive and build the same design
matrix, so the coefficients should match the table the Python notebook
saved, up to rounding. This chunk checks:

```{r parity, eval=TRUE}
python_its <- read_csv(file.path(dirname(SHARED_ARCHIVE), "its_results.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

parity <- tibble(term = its_table$term,
                 r = its_table$estimate,
                 python = python_its$coef) |>
  mutate(difference = r - python)
parity

if (ARCHIVE == SHARED_ARCHIVE) {
  stopifnot("R and Python ITS estimates disagree" = all(abs(parity$difference) < 1e-6))
}
```

```{r its-plot, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
its_plot_data <- its_data |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(its_fit),
    counterfactual = coefs[["intercept"]] + coefs[["trend"]] * t
  )

ggplot(its_plot_data, aes(week)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = n), color = "lightsteelblue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "navy", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = counterfactual), color = "gray40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = paste("Interrupted time series:", TREATED),
       subtitle = "Dashed gray: pre-trend extended as counterfactual") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**How to read this plot.** The gray dashed line is the counterfactual,
the pre-event trend extended as if November 5 had never happened. The
navy line is the model's fit, which is allowed to break at the event.
The vertical gap between the two at the event date is the level shift
(β₂); the way that gap changes over the following months is the slope
change (β₃) at work, small here, so the gap stays roughly constant. The
causal estimate is that gap. Every ITS estimate you report should be
drawn this way: if the picture does not persuade, the coefficient table
will not either.

Notice too that the counterfactual slopes *downward*, because the
pre-event trend does. Extended far enough it would cross zero and predict negative
posts, which is impossible. A linear model of counts has no floor;
modeling log counts, or using Poisson regression (`glm(family =
poisson)`), builds one in.

### An honest aside: autocorrelation

OLS standard errors assume the residuals (the model's week-by-week
errors) are independent of one another. Time series residuals rarely
are: a busy week tends to be followed by a busy week and a quiet one by
a quiet one. This serial dependence is called **autocorrelation**,
because the series is correlated *with a lagged copy of itself*, and it
makes OLS standard errors too small and p-values too confident (the
coefficients themselves are still unbiased). The **Durbin–Watson statistic**
diagnoses this: values near 2 mean no first-order autocorrelation,
values well below 2 mean positive autocorrelation. The standard fix keeps
the OLS coefficients and replaces the standard errors with
**heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC)**, or
Newey–West, errors:

```{r hac, eval=TRUE}
resids <- residuals(its_fit)
dw <- sum(diff(resids)^2) / sum(resids^2)
round(dw, 3)  # 2 = no autocorrelation; < 2 = positive autocorrelation

if (requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  lmtest::coeftest(its_fit, vcov = sandwich::NeweyWest(its_fit, lag = 4, prewhite = FALSE))
} else {
  message("Install the sandwich and lmtest packages for HAC standard errors.")
}
```

With a Durbin–Watson statistic of `r round(dw, 2)`, far below 2, the
correction matters. The level shift stays clearly distinguishable from
zero, but neither the pre-event trend nor the trend change does. The
defensible claim is a *step*; the data cannot tell us whether the slope
changed.

These standard errors match the Python notebook's exactly, but only
because of `prewhite = FALSE`. sandwich's `NeweyWest()` *pre-whitens*
the residuals by default (it fits an autoregression to them first),
while statsmodels does not. HAC estimates depend on choices like this,
and on the lag length, so always report which estimator you used:
"robust standard errors" alone doesn't pin down a number. (Fancier
options, such as ARIMA error structures or GLS, exist; Bernal et al.
2017 in the references is a practical ITS tutorial.)

ITS has one big blind spot: it cannot tell the event apart from
**anything else that changed at the same moment**. If posting rose
because of the election news cycle itself rather than the platform
migration, ITS on one account cannot distinguish those. For that we need
a comparison group.

## 6. Difference-in-differences

The **difference-in-differences (DiD)** design adds a comparison unit
that experienced the same calendar time (the same news cycle, the same
seasonality) but not the treatment. The estimate is the *difference of
two differences*:

DiD = (ȳ<sub>T,post</sub> − ȳ<sub>T,pre</sub>) − (ȳ<sub>C,post</sub> − ȳ<sub>C,pre</sub>)

Whatever would have happened to *everyone* (the comparison group's
change) gets subtracted off, isolating the treated unit's extra change.
The identifying assumption is **parallel trends**: absent the event, the
treated and comparison series would have moved in parallel. That
assumption *is* the design, so restate it slowly. We are not assuming
the two accounts are similar in level (ours differ by an order of
magnitude), only that their *changes over time* would have matched had
the event not occurred, so that the comparison unit's before–after
change can stand in for the treated unit's unobservable counterfactual
change.

DiD is the most widely used quasi-experimental design in the social
sciences; its most famous application is Card & Krueger's (1994)
minimum-wage study, and it gets a gentle chapter in each free textbook:
[Chapter 18 of *The Effect*](https://theeffectbook.net/ch-DifferenceinDifference.html)
and [Chapter 9 of the *Mixtape*](https://mixtape.scunning.com/09-difference_in_differences).
Before estimating anything, a DiD analysis must show the **pre-trend
plot**: do the two series move in parallel before the event?

```{r pretrends, eval=TRUE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
comparison_weekly <- weekly_counts(comparison_posts)

bind_rows(
  mutate(treated_weekly, account = TREATED),
  mutate(comparison_weekly, account = COMPARISON)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, n, color = account)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = EVENT, color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Actions per week",
       title = "Pre-trend plot: treated vs. comparison account") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Squint at the pre-event period and form your own judgment; we will
return to this plot critically in a moment. The DiD estimate can be
computed two equivalent ways, and seeing both
demystifies the regression: first as arithmetic on the 2×2 table of
means, then as the interaction coefficient in a regression, which adds
standard errors. As in the Python notebook, the panel keeps only the
**weeks both accounts have in common**, so it is balanced:

```{r did, eval=TRUE}
# (Base R's intersect() drops the Date class, so filter with %in% instead)
common_weeks <- treated_weekly$week[treated_weekly$week %in% comparison_weekly$week]

panel <- bind_rows(
  mutate(treated_weekly, treated = 1L),
  mutate(comparison_weekly, treated = 0L)
) |>
  filter(week %in% common_weeks) |>
  mutate(post = as.integer(week >= EVENT),
         treated_post = treated * post)

means <- panel |>
  group_by(treated, post) |>
  summarise(mean_actions = mean(n), .groups = "drop")
means

did_by_hand <- with(means,
  (mean_actions[treated == 1 & post == 1] - mean_actions[treated == 1 & post == 0]) -
  (mean_actions[treated == 0 & post == 1] - mean_actions[treated == 0 & post == 0]))

did_fit <- lm(n ~ treated + post + treated_post, data = panel)
did_table <- broom::tidy(did_fit) |>
  mutate(term = c("intercept", "treated", "post", "treated_post"))
did_table
```

The `treated_post` coefficient,
**`r sprintf("%.1f", did_table$estimate[did_table$term == "treated_post"])`**,
equals the by-hand difference of differences
(`r sprintf("%.1f", did_by_hand)`). It is almost exactly the ITS level
shift, because the comparison account's own before–after change
(`post`, `r sprintf("%+.2f", did_table$estimate[did_table$term == "post"])`)
is close to zero. Reading the other coefficients: `intercept` is the
comparison account's pre-event weekly average, `treated` is how much
more active the treated account already was before the event, and `post`
is the comparison account's before–after change, the "what happened to
everyone" term.

### Why this DiD should not be believed

Here is the part of the analysis that matters most, and that a
dishonest write-up would omit. **`bsky.app` is a terrible comparison
group**, for at least three reasons:

1. **It was also treated.** `bsky.app` is the platform's own account.
   During the November surge the Bluesky team was posting welcome
   threads, feature announcements, and status updates *because of the
   very event we are studying*. A comparison unit must be unaffected by
   the treatment; ours sits at the epicenter. In this archive, though,
   `bsky.app` barely moves week to week, so the comparison subtracts
   almost nothing and the DiD collapses into a before–after comparison
   of one account. That is the opposite failure: a comparison too flat
   to absorb the shared shock (the election news cycle) that a newsroom
   certainly experienced.
2. **Parallel trends is visibly violated.** A platform's communications
   account and a national newsroom do not share data-generating
   processes. Their pre-event levels differ by more than an order of
   magnitude, and their movements track product launches versus the news
   cycle. Nothing about one line tells us what the other would have done
   absent the election.
3. **One unit per arm.** With a single treated and a single comparison
   unit, we cannot separate "the effect of the event" from anything
   idiosyncratic that happened to either account that month. Credible
   DiD designs use many units per arm, with uncertainty clustered at the
   unit level.

We chose this comparison deliberately: seeing the assumption fail on
real data teaches more than a sanitized example where it silently holds.
The estimate above is a worked *mechanical* example of DiD, not a
defensible causal estimate.

## 7. Building a better comparison group: matching on profile covariates

A principled comparison pool: accounts similar to the treated unit on
observables. The candidates are one page of the accounts the Times
follows ([`bs_get_follows()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_follows.html)), with their profile
statistics from `bs_get_profile()`. Here is nearest-neighbor matching on (logged) followers,
posts, and account age. We log the heavy-tailed counts so one
mega-account doesn't dominate, standardize each feature with `scale()`
(subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation, so all three are in
comparable units), and rank candidates by Euclidean distance to the
treated account. Matches are reported by rank rather than by handle:
most candidates are individual journalists, and we shouldn't rank named
people.

```{r matching, eval=bsky_authed}
candidates <- bs_get_follows(TREATED, limit = 50)

pool <- bs_get_profile(c(TREATED, head(candidates$handle, 24))) |>
  mutate(account_age_days = as.numeric(
    difftime(now("UTC"), ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE), units = "days"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(followers_count), !is.na(account_age_days))

features <- pool |>
  transmute(handle,
            log_followers = log1p(followers_count),
            log_posts = log1p(posts_count),
            account_age_days) |>
  mutate(across(-handle, \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))))

target <- features |> filter(handle == TREATED)

features |>
  filter(handle != TREATED) |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((log_followers - target$log_followers)^2 +
                         (log_posts - target$log_posts)^2 +
                         (account_age_days - target$account_age_days)^2)) |>
  left_join(select(pool, handle, followers_count, posts_count),
            by = "handle") |>
  slice_min(distance, n = 5) |>
  transmute(match_rank = row_number(), followers_count, posts_count, distance)
```

Read the result before trusting it. Even the nearest matches have a small
fraction of the Times' audience. Matching can only choose among the
candidates you give it, and a pool drawn from the accounts a newsroom
follows contains its reporters, not its peer institutions. A better pool
would be other national news organizations. Even then, a real study
would match on covariates measured *before* the event (`posts` and
`followers` here are measured today, after the treatment, and
conditioning on post-treatment variables is itself a bias), collect
dozens of matched accounts per treated account, verify parallel
pre-trends empirically, and only then estimate. See the
[MatchIt](https://kosukeimai.github.io/MatchIt/) package for the
industrial version.

And we still should not overclaim. Matching makes accounts comparable on
what we can **observe**; the November surge "treated" essentially
everyone on Bluesky to some degree, so a fully untreated control may not
exist *on this platform at all*. Designs researchers used for this
problem on Twitter include comparison groups from a different platform,
accounts in unaffected countries or time zones, or dose-response designs
(accounts more versus less exposed to the migration wave). The hard part
of causal inference is never the regression; it is the argument for the
counterfactual.

## 8. Keyword volume around an event

Account histories are one lens on an event; **keyword volume** is
another.
[`bs_search_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_search_posts.html)
(the R wrapper for
[`app.bsky.feed.searchPosts`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.searchPosts))
accepts `since` and `until` windows, so issuing one search per week and
counting the results builds a topic's time series, exactly how
researchers built event timelines from Twitter's search API
(González-Bailón et al. 2011 tracked protest hashtags this way). Two
cautions: search queries an **index**, not the full network history, so
deletions and opt-outs create survivorship bias; and capping each window
at 1,000 results turns high-volume weeks into a censored measure, so for
popular keywords treat the series as a floor, not a count. Capped to
stay polite:

```{r keyword-volume, eval=bsky_authed, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
edges <- seq(as_date("2024-10-01"), as_date("2024-12-31"), by = "week")

volume <- map2_int(head(edges, -1), tail(edges, -1), \(from, to) {
  hits <- tryCatch(
    bs_search_posts("twitter",
                    since = format(from, "%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z"),
                    until = format(to, "%Y-%m-%dT00:00:00Z"),
                    limit = 1000),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  Sys.sleep(0.2)
  if (is.null(hits)) NA_integer_ else nrow(hits)
})

tibble(week = tail(edges, -1), posts = volume) |>
  ggplot(aes(week, posts)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as_date("2024-11-05"),
             color = "#DC143C", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Posts per week (capped at 1,000)",
       title = "Weekly volume of posts matching 'twitter'") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 9. Saving and reloading the data

Collection took nearly five hundred API requests; analysis should not
require repeating it. The archive and its metadata (collection date,
accounts, event date, stopping rule, requests per account) were saved
the moment they were collected, because live feeds change and a result
that cannot be tied to a collection date cannot be checked. Here we save
the two *derived* tables beside this document, daily counts for both
accounts and the tidy ITS coefficients, so the headline results can be
checked without rerunning anything. (R outputs in `RMarkdown/` are not
committed to the repository; the shared archive lives with the Python
notebook.)

```{r save, eval=TRUE}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

daily_both <- bind_rows(
  mutate(daily_counts(treated_posts), account = TREATED),
  mutate(daily_counts(comparison_posts), account = COMPARISON)
)

write_csv(daily_both, "data/daily_counts.csv")
write_csv(its_table, "data/its_results.csv")

reloaded <- read_csv("data/daily_counts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(reloaded) == nrow(daily_both)
```

## 10. Research design: what it takes to claim causation

Step back from the mechanics. Both designs in this document are
**quasi-experimental**: nobody randomized accounts into "experience the
November surge" and "don't". Instead we leaned on a *natural
experiment* (an event with sharp, externally determined timing) and on
design assumptions that substitute for randomization. Those assumptions
are where causal claims live or die. The recurring **threats to
validity**:

* **Selection.** Who is in the treated group, and why? Our treated
  account is on Bluesky because a major newsroom chose to invest in the
  platform, a decision that may itself have responded to the audience
  surge, which makes "the event" and "the newsroom's strategy" hard to
  pull apart. Effects estimated on self-selected units do not generalize
  to units that chose differently.
* **Anticipation.** Treatments with announced timing leak backward.
  Users disaffected with X were drifting to Bluesky throughout 2024; if
  behavior shifts *before* the event date, the "pre" period is
  contaminated. (The weeks just before the event line in Section 4 are a
  *dip*, which raises the opposite worry: a rebound from a low point
  would look like an effect.)
* **Concurrent shocks.** The election was not only a migration trigger;
  it was a massive news event that changed everyone's posting,
  everywhere. ITS cannot separate co-timed causes at all; DiD can only
  if the comparison group absorbs the shared shock, which requires the
  comparison to be exposed to the news but not the migration.
* **Parallel trends / counterfactual credibility.** ITS assumes the
  pre-trend would have continued; DiD assumes the comparison's change
  reveals the treated counterfactual. Section 6 showed how visibly this
  can fail. Pre-trend plots, placebo events (rerun the ITS on a date
  when nothing happened: a significant "effect" there is a red flag),
  and multiple comparison units are the standard diagnostics.

This is why **correlation-only claims fail**: "posting rose after the
election" is consistent with the event causing the rise, with a
pre-existing trend, with seasonality, with a concurrent shock, and with
regression to the mean after a lull. A design's job is to rule those out
one by one, and a write-up's job is to say plainly which ones it could
not rule out.

## Ethics and limitations

**Ethics.** Posting histories are public, but assembling someone's
complete three-year behavioral trace (when they sleep, when they work,
when they go quiet) is more intrusive than reading any individual post,
and timestamp analysis can reveal patterns (time zone, schedule, life
disruptions) that users never chose to disclose. This document studies
two institutional accounts, a national newsroom and the platform's
official account, whose posting is professional output; apply the same
designs to private individuals only with a research justification,
minimal fields, and aggregate reporting (the saved archive keeps only
the account, action type, reply flag, and timestamp). The matching
section retrieves other accounts' public profile statistics; report such
covariates in aggregate rather than ranking named individuals. And
remember deletion: users remove posts, so a saved archive is a snapshot.
Record the collection date (we did) and honor deletions when sharing
data.

**Limitations.** Everything here measures *visible platform behavior*,
not underlying attention or attitudes: absence of posting is not absence
of activity (lurking is invisible). Two accounts cannot support
population claims; Bluesky's user base over-represents Twitter migrants
and early adopters, and November 2024 in particular reshaped who is on
the platform at all (a selection effect *caused by* our event of study).
Author feeds exclude deleted posts, so the past is measured with
survivorship bias. Weekly counts treat a one-word repost and a 20-post
thread identically. And our event study has a single treated unit and a
knowingly invalid comparison: it is a teaching design. A publishable
version needs many matched accounts, pre-registered event windows,
placebo tests, and honesty about the threats listed in Section 10.

## Exercises

These extend the document, ordered from small modifications to
mini-analyses. All of them can be done with the data and functions
already loaded above.

1. **Change the time zone.** Re-run the `timestamps` chunk with a
   different `TZ` (`"Europe/London"` or `"Asia/Tokyo"`; any [IANA zone
   name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones)
   works) and redraw the diurnal profile. The quiet hours should move to
   wherever your chosen zone places New York's night.
2. **Original posts only.** Rebuild `treated_weekly` from
   `filter(treated_posts, action == "post")` and re-fit the ITS. Do the
   level shift and trend change survive this robustness check, or was
   the November surge mostly a *reposting* surge?
3. **Placebo event.** Re-fit the ITS with a fake event date on which
   nothing notable happened, say `as_date("2024-05-01")`. A
   "significant" level shift at a date you invented is a red flag that
   the design, not the event, is generating findings. Report the placebo
   coefficients side by side with the real ones.
4. **Stress-test the standard errors.** Recompute the HAC errors with
   `lag` of 1, 8, and 12 instead of 4. How sensitive are the conclusions
   about `level_shift` and `trend_change`? There is no single correct lag
   length; reporting the sensitivity is the honest move.
5. **A better comparison account, a better DiD.** Pick the nearest
   matched account from Section 7 (or any account you can argue is a
   better comparison than `bsky.app`), collect its history with the
   `collect_actions()` function from the `refresh` chunk, and redo the
   pre-trend plot and DiD. Is parallel trends more plausible? Does the
   estimate move, and in which direction?
6. **A different event.** Bluesky dropped its invite-code requirement
   and opened public registration on **February 6, 2024**. Re-run the ITS
   around that date. Is there a detectable break, and how does its shape
   (level shift vs. slope change) compare with the November surge?

## Research project ideas

**1. Dose–response in the X-odus.** *Question:* did existing Bluesky
users who were more exposed to the November 2024 migration wave change
their own posting more? *Data:* a sample of accounts created well before
October 2024 (so that being in the sample is not itself caused by the
event), each account's posting history, and an exposure ("dose") measure
such as the share of each account's pre-event follows who were publicly
active in migration conversations (Part 03's network tools help).
*Method:* a continuous-treatment event study (interact the post-event
indicator with dose, or fit separate ITS models by dose tercile) with
HAC or account-clustered standard errors. *Expected challenge:* naive
dose measures (follower growth during the surge) are themselves outcomes
of the event, so the design hinges on a pre-determined exposure proxy
and candid argument about the endogeneity that remains.

**2. Feature launches as interrupted time series.** *Question:* do
platform feature launches (in-app video, DMs, whichever launch is recent
when you read this) change how much and what people post? *Data:*
weekly post volumes and post-type shares (links, images, video, replies)
for a panel of a few hundred accounts sampled *before* the launch,
collected with this part's paging code or platform-wide via Part 10's
Jetstream tools. *Method:* ITS on the aggregate share of posts using the
new feature, with placebo dates before the launch; a staggered rollout
supports a DiD between early- and late-access accounts. *Expected
challenge:* launches are announced in advance and rolled out gradually,
so the "interruption" is fuzzy; reconstruct the timeline from the
[Bluesky blog](https://bsky.social/about/blog) and show the results are
robust to the choice of event date.

**3. News shocks and topical attention with keyword series.**
*Question:* how fast does attention to a sudden news event rise and
decay on Bluesky, and does it crowd out other topics? *Data:* weekly or
daily keyword-volume series built with the authenticated search loop
from Section 8, for event-related keywords and a basket of placebo
keywords unrelated to the event. *Method:* ITS on the event keywords
with the placebo basket as comparison series (a difference-in-differences
in attention), looking for the explosive-onset, slow-decay dynamics
González-Bailón et al. (2011) documented for protest hashtags. *Expected
challenge:* the search index undercounts and the per-window cap censors
high-volume weeks, so the series is a floor rather than a count;
validate a few windows against an independent measure such as Jetstream
sampling.
